item.title: Radio Essay: The Courtyard I Remember
item.summary: A reflective radio essay uses the memory of a childhood courtyard in Tashkent to ask what nostalgia is really a longing for.
item.transcript_text: When I think of childhood, I think of a courtyard in Tashkent. There was a vine growing over a metal frame, a low table where the adults drank tea in the evenings, and a tap that never quite stopped dripping. I remember that courtyard as permanently sunlit, which I know cannot be true. It must have rained. I must have been bored there, and cold, and occasionally miserable. But memory, it seems, is an editor with strong opinions. The word nostalgia was coined centuries ago to describe a kind of illness, a homesickness so severe that it was thought to make soldiers far from home physically unwell. For a long time afterwards it kept a slightly suspicious reputation, as a sentimental longing for a past that never really existed. And there's some truth in that charge. Whole political movements have been built on a polished version of yesterday, one from which the inconvenient details have quietly been removed. Yet I've come to think that nostalgia deserves a more generous hearing. When I remember that courtyard, I'm not really claiming that the past was better. I'm reminding myself that I was once held in place by people who knew me, by a routine, by the sound of one particular tap. Nostalgia, in that sense, is less a longing for a time than for a feeling of belonging. The danger comes only when we mistake one for the other, and try to rebuild the time in the hope of recovering the feeling. The courtyard has since been replaced by an apartment block. I find, somewhat to my surprise, that I don't mind as much as I expected. What I was attached to was never really the vine or the tap. It was who I was, and who was around me, when I sat beneath them.

Memory tends to select and improve the past.
